Radio interferometry plays a crucial role in studying the universe'\'s radio continuum emission. However, traditional correlators used in interferometry have a computational complexity of O(N^2) operations, with a resulting data output of size N, processing time, and storage requirements that are impractical for large-scale, high-precision radio astronomy projects. To address this issue, an innovative FFT-correlator architecture has been developed, leveraging the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to reduce computational complexity to O(N log^2(N)) and achieve significant time savings of up to 100-fold. This paper presents the underlying theory and an implementation of the FFT-correlator, demonstrating its capabilities through real-world applications and highlighting potential applications in radio astronomy and beyond.

In the field of financial time series analysis, generative models like conditional GANs are being explored for their potential to analyze and compare generative patterns. However, these models are limited in their ability to account for the complex interplay between multiple financial variables. To address this limitation, we introduce a new generative model that utilizes a graph neural network to capture the interdependencies between multiple financial variables. This model, known as the Graph Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GC-GAN), uses a dynamic graph to model the interdependencies between variables and conditions on the graph structure to generate time series data. Experimental results on real-world financial time series data demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model in capturing the interdependencies between variables and outperforming existing generative models in terms of predictive accuracy.

We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(2)}(N)$
analytically to three-loop order in QCD for arbitrary values of $N$,
including both single- and double-mass cases in the Larin scheme.
Additionally, the result serves as a crucial transition function for the variable
flavor number scheme at O($\alpha_s^3$) and is expressed using special functions.
We have also provided a detailed comparison with the results obtained using
the momentum space integral equation for the massive QCD evolution kernel.

We developed a novel approach to classify Fermi-LAT blazar candidates, leveraging machine learning techniques with extensive training and by utilizing distinct feature sets. Our analysis focused on two categories: Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars and BL Lacertae Objects, with the goal of creating accurate classification models based on both traditional astrophysical characteristics and machine-extracted features derived from the literature. Our results indicate that this method can effectively distinguish between FSRQs and BL Lacs, with an accuracy of approximately 90%. Moreover, by applying this classification model to the entire Fermi-LAT source list, we generated probability distributions for each source's likelihood of being a BL Lac object.

Social media platforms are now flooded with a variety of user-generated content, 
ranging from short to extended videos, live streams, and interactive 360-degree photos. 
Although existing tools can translate and caption these media, the process is often incomplete 
and fails to account for the unique characteristics of each format. Moreover, existing methods 
are not designed to work together seamlessly, leading to a loss of context in the final output. 
This paper proposes a new system that addresses these limitations by utilizing AI-powered 
technology to create comprehensive translations and captions for immersive multimedia content. 
The system's effectiveness was demonstrated through user testing, which showed that participants 
preferred the translations and captions generated by our method over those generated by Google 
Translate and Facebook, especially for complex 360-degree photos and videos.

This paper introduces a new hypergraph class called hypergraphs of tensors, where each hypergraph is associated with a tensor. A hypergraph and a tensor combine to form a new hypergraph through the tensor join operation, analogous to the matrix join, which is studied in this work. The study focuses on understanding the structural and counting properties of these composite hypergraphs. The tensor join is also applied to examine the hypergraphs within a class of hypergraph families. The tensor join operation offers an alternative to merging smaller hypergraphs to form a larger one, which can be beneficial in computational complexity theory.

The INSIST space telescope is designed to explore the universe with its 2.1-meter mirror, capable of observing near-infrared and mid-infrared wavelengths. This allows scientists to study the universe's formation and evolution, with a focus on understanding the universe's composition and properties. INSIST will be built using a modular design, with a primary structure consisting of a hexagonal mirror cell and a mid-infrared camera. This design will be tested using a laboratory model of the mirror cell, which will be studied using a mid-infrared camera to assess its performance.

In clinical trials, the mixed model repeated measures analysis is commonly used
for assessing the impact of a treatment on continuous outcomes across multiple
time points. The traditional approach treats time as a categorical variable, but
this can lead to issues such as non-normality and overfitting due to
assumptions like sphericity. An alternative method utilizes a continuous time
variable, but this requires a linear model and can be problematic if there are
diseased state time points that don't fit a linear pattern. Our solution is a
mixed model with a piecewise linear representation of time, where we can
easily incorporate categorical variables and handle irregularly spaced time
points. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness using real-world data from
multiple sclerosis trials.

A novel computational method has been developed to identify reaction pathways
between stable states in a complex energy landscape. This approach utilizes the
Onsager-Machlup action, which is based on the principle of minimum energy
occupation, to determine optimal reaction pathways. By applying the principle
of fluctuation dissipation, the action can be expressed in terms of the energy
barrier between stable states. A simple optimization algorithm is employed to
extract the most probable reaction pathway from an ensemble of molecular
dynamics simulations. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through its
application to two systems: a two-dimensional potential energy landscape and
a peptide folding model.

This paper provides local and global estimates for a parabolic complex Monge-Ampere equation, deriving L-infinity and Holder estimates from an a priori perspective. In addition, the research demonstrates the potential for these estimates to be used in constructing solutions for the Kähler-Einstein equation on a compact Kähler manifold without singularities.

Automata theory has traditionally been used to study regular languages, but more complex classes like polyregular functions and transducers have also been explored, particularly in the 1970s and 80s. These functions can be seen as a form of multivariate logic, and it was shown that they are PSPACE-complete. This paper introduces a new class of transducers, called cored polytransducers, which can be restricted to recognize polyregular functions. Surprisingly, this new class is PSPACE-hard as well. Additionally, we examine a related class of transducers called polycore transducers, which can also recognize polyregular functions, and find that it is at least as hard.

This article offers a comprehensive overview of the relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals, specifically in the context of conditional measure flow systems. By leveraging the concept of Riemann-Stieltjes integrals, the article provides a detailed explanation of the relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals, along with a discussion of the conditions necessary for equivalence. A key aspect of the article involves exploring the impact of non-uniqueness of measure flow decomposition and the emergence of 'anti-invariant' components, which do not contribute to the equivalence of Ito and Stratonovich integrals. A notable example illustrates how anti-invariant components arise from non-uniqueness of measure flow decomposition, while a discussion of the anti-invariant components' physical significance and implications concludes the article.

A normal subgroup is termed primitive if it cannot be broken down into the product of smaller normal subgroups. The issue of determining the primitivity of subgroups within a finite group is a complex one, particularly when dealing with subgroups of order two. This paper aims to contribute to that challenge by examining the primitivity of subgroups of finite groups $G$ with a subgroup of order two, specifically by analyzing the properties of these groups in relation to their Sylow subgroups of order two.

The primary goal of semantic parsing is to accurately represent natural language queries in a standardized format.  However, existing research has primarily focused on queries related to a single database schema, whereas real-world applications involve queries from multiple, unrelated domains. To address this challenge, we introduce a new task known as cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic parsing, which aims to leverage general knowledge to accurately represent queries from diverse domains. To achieve this goal, we identify two critical components: domain-agnostic general knowledge and domain-specific application of this knowledge. To address this challenge, we develop a new approach that combines a graph-based neural network with a knowledge-aware module, and evaluate its effectiveness on a new dataset comprising queries from four distinct domains. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, and highlight the importance of both domain-agnostic general knowledge and domain-specific application in cross-domain semantic parsing.

This research addresses the challenge of safely navigating multiple robots within a confined space by minimizing collision risk. A novel approach is proposed, which formulates the collision avoidance problem as a distributionally robust optimization problem to account for uncertainty in robots' trajectories. A robust extension of Conditional Value-at-Risk is introduced to quantify the probability of collision, and an iterative algorithm is developed to solve the problem using a dual decomposition technique. The method is evaluated through simulations involving multiple robots moving autonomously in a rectangular area, and results demonstrate its effectiveness in ensuring collision-free navigation.

Our research presents the first spectroscopic study of the Andromeda XXV dwarf spheroidal galaxy, based on observations made with the Mauna Kea Observatory's APOGEE-4 spectrograph. We successfully obtained spectra for 15 stars, of which 11 were previously identified as members of Andromeda XXV. Our analysis yielded reliable velocity measurements for 9 of these stars, revealing a systemic velocity of $-77.8 \pm 2.4$ km s$^{-1}$. This result aligns with previous photometric metallicity and radial velocity measurements, as well as APOGEE photometric metallicity estimates. Our findings also include the determination of radial velocities for 4 new candidate members of Andromeda XXV.

In massive machine-type communications, grant-free access with short, randomized transmissions can minimize signaling overhead and reduce data exchange between devices and the central node. However, the resulting complex multi-user channel is challenging to decode. To address this issue, we propose a novel, low-complexity detection method that leverages a tensor completion approach with a unique structure that can handle the channel's multi-user property. The method involves two stages: an initial stage that resolves channel coefficients for active devices, and a second stage that determines data lengths and identifies inactive devices within the same detection space. The method's performance is evaluated through simulations, demonstrating superior results compared to existing solutions.

A novel, simplified approach has been developed to model the thermodynamic properties of moist air. This method utilizes thermodynamic potentials, leveraging the chemical potential's inherent advantages while minimizing the need for complex and computationally intensive calculations involving water vapor's various liquid and gasephase forms. The approach's core consists of a set of concise, empirically derived formulas for thermodynamic potential's partial derivatives, which are then used to derive the complete set of thermodynamic potential equations. These equations, in turn, enable the calculation of thermodynamic potential's value and its gradient, ultimately facilitating the determination of moisture flux. The new method has been successfully tested against a reference solution derived from the fundamental thermodynamic principles and has been implemented in the Met Office's Unified Model, with promising results during a simulation of a tropical disturbance.

We introduce a novel algebraic structure, the unitary edge algebra, which is a unique type of algebra that can be based on $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$ and has an additional underlying structure. This algebra is then utilized to create the concept of the unitary edge quantum group, which is a generalization of the quantum group $\mathbb{U}_q(\mathfrak{g})$. Furthermore, we establish that the unitary edge quantum group can be expressed as a $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$-algebra through the process of specialization from $\mathbb{C}$ to $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$.

Recent advancements in spoken dialogue systems have highlighted the limitations of relying solely on top-N ASR hypotheses. To address these shortfalls, we propose utilizing confusion networks to represent multiple ASR outcomes. However, current methods face challenges in efficiently scaling to meet the needs of modern systems. To overcome this, we introduce a novel approach that leverages a pre-trained language model to selectively prune unnecessary paths within the confusion network, thereby reducing its size and complexity. This method not only accelerates inference but also enhances the system's interpretability and resilience to out-of-vocabulary words and semantic errors. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in producing high-quality dialogue responses of comparable quality to baseline methods, but with significantly reduced computational requirements.

Building on the work of Maruyama, we derive and demonstrate explicit formulas for enumerative invariants of semistable coherent sheaves on a complex projective curve, specifically when the curve has genus g and a point P where the fiber functor exhibits tameness. This development subsumes Maruyama's results for enumerative invariants of vector bundles and sheaves with specific properties, including those that are of negative degree and have a certain slope. Furthermore, we establish that the invariants we calculate align with the predictions made by the Bogomolny-Myers-Perry theory.

A specific access structure, known as G_2, is defined with two participants, resulting in a secret sharing scheme with two components. By examining the family of all such schemes for a fixed number of shares, researchers identified a particular structure that encompasses all possible secret sharing schemes for this access structure, regardless of the number of shares, as long as this number is at least three. This structure, known as the universal access structure for G_2, has a unique set of properties that can be precisely defined.

Our approach to measuring entanglement in polarization qubit pairs yields highly accurate results, with optimal precision attainable by employing the quantum Fisher information. We develop a simplified method to calculate this information, expressing it in terms of the qubit's Fock states. Our method is particularly valuable when analyzing large numbers of qubit pairs, as it allows for efficient simulation of many qubits in each pair. We demonstrate that the quantum Fisher information can be approximated using a specific subset of the qubit's Fock states, and that this approximation becomes increasingly precise as the number of qubit pairs grows.

Plasma turbulence in the magnetized plasma frame is characterized by small-scale coherent structures known as solitons and jets, which form through the nonlinear interaction of turbulent modes. These coherent modes are influenced by the parallel electric field associated with plasma turbulence, causing electrons to move and generate electron current fluctuations. This process is linked to the parallel currents carried by the coherent structures, which can impact the global properties of plasma turbulence. This study focuses on the coherent structures in collisionless plasma turbulence, specifically solitons and jets, and their role in parallel currents. We examine the electron current fluctuations generated by these coherent structures and their scaling properties, which are compared to the total electron current fluctuations. This comparison reveals that coherent structures contribute significantly to the total electron current fluctuations, with the ratio of coherent to total electron current fluctuations reaching up to 0.5. This finding implies that coherent structures are responsible for a substantial portion of the electron current fluctuations in plasma turbulence.

Continual learning, particularly in the context of image classification tasks, has garnered significant interest in recent years. One promising approach to addressing the challenges of forgetting and preventing catastrophic interference involves leveraging pretraining. This study investigates the efficacy of utilizing a "frozen" pretrained model for image classification tasks via continual learning. Notably, we demonstrate that even a frozen model, without undergoing further optimization, can facilitate significant reductions in forgetting when paired with an experience replay strategy that utilizes random sampling.

Hate speech on social media has severe real-world consequences, including promoting violence and hatred against marginalized groups. As a result, researchers have been working to develop effective methods for identifying hate speech, and this paper contributes to those efforts by proposing a new approach that combines linguistic analysis with visual analysis of social media posts. Our approach uses a neural network to analyze the visual components of a post, including images and video, and this can help to reveal content that is encoded or obscured. By combining linguistic and visual analysis, we can improve our ability to identify hate speech, and this can be demonstrated through experiments on multiple datasets.

We investigate the dynamics of a typical inhibitory ring network composed of IIFN neurons, where the neurons receive inputs from an average number of excitatory neurons whose connection strengths follow a type of distribution. By analyzing the neuron model developed by Bouchaud et al. in detail, we derive a simplified equation describing the neurons' voltage evolution. Our analysis reveals that increasing the variability of the input distribution has a significant impact on the oscillations within the network, broadening it leads to the disappearance of the oscillations. Furthermore, we explore the robustness of the oscillations in a related network model, where the neurons are randomly connected, and find that the oscillations are robust to changes in the distribution of synaptic weights when the distribution is not too concentrated.

Recent advancements in Neural-Aided Program Repair (NAPR) have demonstrated the potential of combining Neural Networks with Program Repair, particularly in generating syntactically valid patches for buggy code. However, the reliance on GANs in NAPR has hindered the development of practical applications, as it often produces low-quality, semantically flawed patches. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new framework, PatchGAN, which leverages GANs in a more controlled manner to produce better- quality patches. By integrating PatchGAN with a repair function that utilizes a Transformer network, we achieve improved results on two repair tasks, including higher accuracy on the DeepRepair dataset and improved performance on the DeepRepair-v2 dataset.

This paper introduces a new model for interference channels, which can be fully decoded at any point within its capacity range using a simple, universal coding technique. The technique involves combining standard Gaussian coding methods with a novel method for interference mitigation developed by Khatri-Rao product, which the authors show can be optimized to achieve optimal interference levels. The paper's model builds on previous work by M. A. Ghosh and J. M. Kahn, who established a lower bound on interference levels that can be fully decoded. The paper's main contribution is to show that this lower bound is not necessary and that more extreme interference levels can also be fully decoded. The paper's results have significant implications for the design of interference-mitigating techniques and provide a new perspective on the relationship between interference levels and decoding performance.

Investigating the nuclear Equation-of-State through flow analysis in heavy-ion collisions is a well-established method. However, the relationship between the nuclear EoS and flow coefficients is influenced by factors such as the collision energy, stage of the collision, and multi-particle correlations. This study examines how the nuclear EoS affects the fourth flow coefficient, $\nu_4$, and identifies energy and centrality trends in $\nu_4$ that are insensitive to the EoS.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread devastation and economic loss, with over 6 million reported fatalities worldwide. Early detection of COVID-19 is crucial for effective management and in preventing a further surge in cases, as well as reducing the burden on healthcare systems. To facilitate this, we have developed a deep learning-based model that utilizes chest X-rays for COVID-19 diagnosis. Our model, which integrates the strengths of ResNet, Inception-ResNet, and Inception architectures, demonstrates impressive performance capabilities, with a top-tier ranking on the COVID-19 Image Dataset Comparison Information on Kaggle. Our model's exceptional accuracy and efficiency make it a valuable resource for medical professionals and researchers working on COVID-19 diagnosis and detection.

Graph neural networks have gained significant attention in recent years, particularly for tasks involving wireless communication systems. However, current graph neural networks face several limitations, including their inability to handle non-stationary environments, difficulty in modeling complex relationships between nodes, and inefficiency in processing large amounts of data. To address these issues, this research introduces a novel framework called the Learning-based Wireless Graph Neural Network (LW-GNN). The LW-GNN framework leverages a combination of techniques, including a graph generator, a node encoder, a relationship modeler, and a node predictor, to develop a more robust and efficient GNN model. The proposed model employs a graph generator to dynamically adjust the network structure in response to changing environmental conditions. Additionally, a node encoder utilizing a multi-head attention mechanism is designed to capture complex node-to-node relationships, and a relationship modeler is introduced to model these relationships more effectively. Finally, a node predictor is developed to combine the information from each component and produce the desired output. The effectiveness of the proposed LW-GNN framework is demonstrated through its application in a real-world wireless communication system, where it outperforms existing GNN models in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

The country's largest, predominantly black region, Brazil, faces significant issues with violent deaths, with homicide being the leading cause of mortality among young people under the age of 35. To better understand the scope of this problem, researchers conducted a comprehensive analysis of autopsies performed at a major public hospital in Salvador, Bahia, over a period of nearly two years. The study involved reviewing 1,514 autopsies, focusing on those with a final diagnosis of death due to homicide, and it revealed that the majority of victims were male, with a median age of 28. The most common causes of death were related to firearms, with a significant proportion of victims being under the influence of alcohol at the time of death. The study's findings have important implications for public policy and clinical practice, and they highlight the need for further research into the broader social and cultural contexts surrounding violent deaths in Brazil.

We investigate the problem of minimizing a smooth, strongly-convex function with non-euclidean geometry. We demonstrate that a stochastic gradient descent algorithm with step sizes decreasing exponentially can achieve a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(\log(T)/\sqrt{L})$, where $T$ is the number of iterations, $L$ is the smoothness parameter, and $\log(T)$ is the complexity parameter. This result is particularly noteworthy as it does not rely on any structural assumptions about the Hessian's eigenvalues. We also show that this rate is optimal for non-euclidean settings. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to the mini-batch stochastic gradient descent, revealing that a step size schedule with a power greater than 1 can guarantee a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K} + \log(T)/\sqrt{L \cdot K})$, where $K$ is the mini-batch size.

We suggest a new mechanism to address the strong-CP problem, utilizing a $U(1)_R$ symmetry. In this framework, the symmetry is broken down into a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ subgroup, which is then incorporated into the Standard Model. The mechanism relies on a new, heavy pseudoscalar boson, which can be detected at future high-energy colliders, such as the FCC-hh.

The understanding of memory storage in biological systems is heavily rooted in equilibrium thermodynamics, yet living organisms function in non-equilibrium states. This paper presents a new approach to studying memory in biological and artificial neural systems, drawing from the principles of non-equilibrium thermodynamics. It introduces a model for a biological neuron's energy flow and proposes a non-equilibrium memory storage mechanism, supported by experimental data. Furthermore, the model is applied to artificial neural networks, revealing that non-equilibrium conditions can lead to improved performance in both linear and logistic classification tasks.

We introduce DexGraspNet, a comprehensive dataset of 1 million grasping configurations suitable for a variety of research applications related to robotic dexterity. The dataset is comprised of 10 dexterous finger models captured through 10 cameras, providing a detailed representation of hand-object interactions. The data was collected using a semi-automated approach, leveraging a single robot arm to capture images from various viewpoints. The dataset is accompanied by ground truth information regarding object pose, hand orientation, and finger tips. The development of DexGraspNet is a significant advancement in the field of robotic dexterous grasping, offering several key benefits, including a large scale, diverse, and easily accessible data collection process. The use of a standardized hand model and camera setup facilitates data comparison and extension. The incorporation of a semi-automated data collection approach enables researchers to efficiently collect data for a variety of objects. The dataset is available for public use at https://dex-grasp-net.github.io.

A novel MRI technique has been developed to create clear images despite patient movement. By using data from the MRI scanner's built-in sensors to track a patient's respiratory pattern, images can be reconstructed to freeze motion at any point. However, the traditional approach to this problem, known as a 4D MRI scan, is very time-consuming and can take several minutes to complete. In an effort to reduce this problem, a new technique called a 'free-breathing, free-flow' MRI method has been developed. This method uses data from the MRI scanner's built-in sensors to create a model of a patient's respiratory pattern and then uses this information to create clear images. A new technique called a 'deep learning network' has been used to develop this new method, and it has been tested using data from 20 patients. The results show that the new method is successful in creating clear images in just a few seconds, and it is as effective as the traditional 4D MRI method.

Knowledge distillation is a well-known method for model compression that enables a smaller model to mimic the behavior of a larger, high-performing model by training it on the same data. This technique has been widely adopted in computer vision, but its application in natural language processing has been limited due to the difficulty in designing a direct similarity comparison function between word embeddings. This paper proposes a new approach to distillation in NLP, using a similarity metric derived from the word embeddings' covariance matrices, which are estimated from the inner product of the embeddings. This method is applied to the BERT architecture and achieves promising results, with the smaller model outperforming the larger model on GLUE tasks after distillation.

Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers are defined, and their respective level set foliations are examined. The equivalence of these functions topologically implies the topological equivalence of their foliations, but it does not necessarily follow that the hyperbolic structure of the foliation is preserved. However, under specific conditions where one function is a local submersion, the topological equivalence of the functions does indeed imply the topological equivalence of their hyperbolic structures.

Ecosystems in dry landscapes experience increased vulnerability to degradation due to grazing, yet the impact of grazing is not uniformly distributed. In fact, areas with more vegetation tend to experience lower grazing pressure, while areas with less vegetation tend to experience higher grazing pressure. This phenomenon is observed in a study on a semi-arid grassland ecosystem, where a model of a grazing system revealed that spatial patterns of vegetation can significantly influence the overall grazing dynamics. In particular, areas with more vegetation can act as a buffer, reducing the impact of grazing pressure on other areas. This can lead to a self-regulating system where areas with more vegetation help protect areas with less vegetation from overgrazing. This mechanism is a key factor in the maintenance of spatial patterns of vegetation in ecosystems that are subject to grazing pressure.

We've developed a novel CountSketch technique modification to create a more accurate and unbiased estimator for calculating the degree distribution of a given graph. Our method employs CountSketch sketches, which are then analyzed through a degree-based random walk. This process enables the calculation of the degree distribution by dividing the graph's vertices into buckets based on their degrees and applying CountSketch sketches to each bucket. To achieve this, we've introduced a new CountSketch estimator that uses random walk samples to determine the number of vertices in each bucket, rather than relying on the original estimator's random walk samples from the entire graph. By doing so, we've established a more accurate and efficient method for estimating the degree distribution.

We introduce a Python-based quantum Monte Carlo program that utilizes the auxiliary-field QMC method for calculating electronic excitation energies and properties of molecules and clusters. The program is designed to be efficient, flexible, and user-friendly, with a range of computational and memory optimizations that improve its performance on a variety of computer architectures. The program's performance is demonstrated by calculating excitation spectra for a range of molecules and clusters, with particular emphasis on its ability to handle challenging systems on a variety of computer hardware.

This study explores the application of cooperative game theory to analyze high-frequency trading (HFT) among a group of traders, with the aim of identifying a fair and efficient solution for all. By modeling the HFT market as a network where traders interact with each other and the market, the study defines a game theory property called superadditivity. It also introduces the concept of a frequency-based network, which represents the traders' interactions through the purchase and sale of assets at various frequencies. To address the issue of how to fairly distribute trading profits among members, the study proposes a cooperative game theory approach, using the Shapley value as a reference point for assessing individual contributions and efficiency.

In a study on the simultaneous double auction mechanism, bidders' private estimates of item value are drawn independently from a common distribution when items are identical, or independently with common distribution for one item and another distribution for another item when items are distinct. To achieve truthful bidding, a price per item is set before bidding. The goal is to determine the optimal price that maximizes profit, which involves analyzing the expected revenue and the impact of price on demand. By modeling the expected revenue as a function of price, and using a dynamic programming approach, an optimal price can be determined through backward induction. The approach is computationally feasible for situations where the distribution of value is discrete, or when a closed-form expression for revenue can be obtained for continuous distributions.

To enhance the specificity of summaries generated by neural models, we propose an approach that involves fine-tuning a pre-trained decoder with entity chains extracted from the source text. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in the context of summarization tasks and show that it can be adapted to other tasks requiring specific information retention. We also introduce a new dataset for summarization with entity chains, and our results indicate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art models in retaining specific information in summaries.

This research introduces new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with multiple variables, where these conditions are based on partial differential equations with a polynomial coefficient. We provide detailed proof of these conditions, which outperform existing ones in terms of flexibility and applicability. We also establish the relationship between these conditions and those of Hadamard, where we discover that certain classical theorems can be viewed as specific instances of our main result.

Human vocal synchronization in social interactions holds significant value in understanding interpersonal dynamics, as it provides insight into an individual's cognitive behaviors and emotions. This study investigates the connection between social abilities and vocal synchronization skills in children on the autism spectrum. An innovative method for measuring synchronization has been developed, which takes into account the unique characteristics of autism spectrum disorder. This approach involves analyzing the similarity between the duration and timing of vocal expressions rather than their absolute values. A large dataset consisting of conversations between children with autism and non-autism controls has been used to validate the new metric and identify distinct patterns in their conversational styles.

This study demonstrates the application of a realizability technique to the quantum lambda calculus, yielding a comprehensive framework for inferring typing in a quantum lambda calculus with implicit typing. The proposed framework is built upon a fundamental typing relation that is inherently more lenient than explicit typing, allowing for the derivation of typing relations without explicit use of typing assumptions. The application of this relation to the lambda calculus extended with quantum branching and measurement operators showcases its utility in this context. The developed typing relation is particularly adept at handling the measurement operator, enabling the derivation of typing relations even when assumptions are not explicitly used. The study also explores the connection between the proposed typing relation and a traditional typing relation that is more restrictive in its use of typing assumptions.

We examine the quasiparticle energy spectrum using exact diagonalization for systems with 2, 3, and 4 electrons under magnetic fields, comparing the results to the predictions of Laughlin and composite fermions theories. The latter incorporates a scaling transformation to account for its energy spectrum. Our findings show that for two electrons, the composite fermions' energy spectrum aligns with the Laughlin theory after a field scaling transformation, achieving a precise match. However, this is not the case for systems with three or four electrons, where the composite fermions' energy spectra do not match the observed energies when adjusted for magnetic field scaling.

We offer a novel, highly efficient numerical solution strategy for a specific type of glaciological problem, specifically Stokes variational inequalities. This problem is a more complex version of Stokes equations, accounting for frictional contact and free boundaries, and can be found in various applications such as ice sheet modeling. Our approach simplifies the solution process by transforming the inequalities into a system of partial differential equations with constraints. We use a non-conforming finite element method to approximate this system, and provide a thorough error analysis for both the semi-discrete and fully discrete schemes. Our numerical results confirm the theoretical findings and offer valuable insights into the model's behavior.

We conducted a study of starbursting galaxies at redshifts of 2-4 using data from ALMA observations, focusing on the outflows of gas and dust. We found that the mass flux of the outflows increases with the density of star formation, but at a slower rate than in other galaxies. We also discovered that the outflows of dust are less powerful than those of gas, and that the mass of the dust outflow is much lower than the mass of the gas outflow. We found that the mass of the dust outflow can be predicted by measuring the amount of gas being expelled, and that the rate of dust production in these galaxies is much lower than in the Milky Way.

The connection between the initial anisotropic shape of the collision geometry and the final anisotropic flow of particles is investigated in detail through the VhESPHERES model, which incorporates the effects of viscosity and is sensitive to initial conditions. The model accurately reproduces the centrality trends of flow fluctuations in Au+Au collisions at 200 GeV and Cu+Cu collisions at 62.4 GeV. The model also reveals that the initial anisotropic geometry of the collision is directly reflected in the final anisotropic flow of particles, with the exception of the third-order triangular flow which is influenced by the initial shape of the collision geometry.

This research introduces a novel approach to synchronizing a large group of robots, or swarm, through a real-time communication system that utilizes a digital display to coordinate the robots' movements. The proposed method employs a software tool that generates a digital representation of the swarm's intended trajectory, or virtual leader, which is displayed on a screen. The robots are equipped with cameras to capture the display image, and a custom algorithm guides each robot to follow the virtual leader, resulting in a synchronized and cohesive physical swarm. The approach is tested using a software simulation and a real-world experiment involving multiple robots, and its effectiveness in producing a coordinated swarm is demonstrated.

Deep neural network training can be inefficient and resource-intensive, particularly when relying on labeled data for fine-tuning.  A novel, unsupervised approach has been developed to leverage depth estimation from unlabeled videos for pre-training, followed by semantic segmentation tasks.  By incorporating a depth estimation task into unsupervised pre-training, it has been demonstrated that this method yields better results on semantic segmentation tasks compared to other pre-training techniques.  Furthermore, it has been observed that this approach can also improve the ability of a network to generalize when fine-tuning is performed with limited labeled data.

This paper presents an enhanced version of Bohr's inequality, which has been expanded to include series of the form $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} z^{f(n)} c_n$. Our investigation supports the claim that $f(n)$ should be a strictly increasing function in order to yield the most expanded version of Bohr's inequality. Furthermore, we have explored the relationship between the norm of the mapping $T$ and the coefficients of the series.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is examined in relation to its asymptotic properties when applied to data sets that contain ties. A comprehensive overview of existing theoretical frameworks for understanding Kendall's tau is presented, along with a discussion of known results and limitations. Furthermore, a novel analytical framework is developed to derive the asymptotic distribution of Kendall's tau in relation to the sample size, which is shown to be influenced by the data's marginal probability distributions and the degree of non-random tautology within the data set. This new framework is validated through the analysis of two distinct types of data, one generated randomly and the other exhibiting non-random characteristics.

The integration of Intelligent Transportation Systems with Edge Intelligence Systems is gaining momentum, transforming traditional transportation systems. A novel Edge Intelligence-based ITS framework is proposed, comprising intelligent edge devices and a cloud-based component, to facilitate real-time data processing and decision-making. This framework is designed to support the development of intelligent transportation systems, including traffic management, route optimization, and accident prevention. A specific ITS application, in-vehicle traffic signal control, is also explored, demonstrating the potential benefits and challenges of this ITS-EIS framework.

The Euler characteristic serves as a fundamental, widely recognized topological attribute with applications in various branches of mathematics. This note aims to provide an overview of the Euler characteristic in the specific context of topological representations for learning tasks.

This research investigates a predator-prey model that takes into account a complex interaction between the two species, incorporating a unique form of response in the prey population that is influenced by the presence of the predator. By analyzing the model's parameters, we examine the boundaries that distinguish different dynamic behaviors, including areas where one species becomes extinct, coexistence occurs, and oscillatory behavior emerges. Furthermore, we identify the boundaries that separate these regions and provide insights into the stability of the system in the stable coexistence state.

The Hirsch Conjecture suggested that a d-dimensional polytope with n faces cannot exceed a diameter of d(n-1)-d. This conjecture has been disputed since 1967 when Mabuchi showed it false. The current knowledge reveals that a d-dimensional simple polytope cannot have a diameter exceeding d(n-1)-d for n>d+3. This knowledge resolves the Hirsch Conjecture for all but the smallest cases.

We explore the concept of k-torsion in associative rings and Nil-groups, and introduce a condition known as the k-torsion condition, which can be applied to these mathematical structures. This condition is particularly noteworthy as it is satisfied by certain classes of associative rings (such as Herstein, Vassiliev, and commutative rings) and Nil-groups. Furthermore, we establish that the k-torsion condition is satisfied by group extensions involving these structures. This investigation also delves into the k-torsion condition in the context of Lie and Jordan algebras, as well as in the broader setting of associative and commutative systems.

This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, off-shell computation for pp -> ttj events, particularly focusing on the dileptonic decay channel, with an approximation based on the narrow width assumption. Our study's findings are highly relevant given the LHC's top priority on measuring the top quark mass with high precision. The numerical results presented in the paper will be made available to the community through a publicly accessible repository.

The widespread adoption of face recognition technology in high-stakes settings has created a critical need for robust testing frameworks. Current evaluation protocols, however, fall short in capturing the true resilience required for these applications. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel protocol that incorporates diverse testing approaches, including the use of adversarial attacks. By applying attacks with varying levels of intensity on images from multiple datasets, we can better assess the face recognition system's performance under challenging conditions. The results of this protocol, known as Adversarial Face Verification Challenge, were presented at the 2021 Face and Visual Content Conference, where a challenge was launched with participating teams. The outcome of this challenge revealed significant performance differences when face recognition systems were subjected to increasing levels of adversarial attacks.

The application of supervised learning in autonomous driving has significant limitations, primarily due to the substantial time and financial costs associated with data annotation. In contrast, semi-supervised learning presents an attractive solution by leveraging large amounts of unlabeled data to improve performance. This study introduces a novel approach to semi-supervised learning in autonomous driving tasks, incorporating a self-training strategy to identify and focus on the most challenging unlabeled samples. A sample selection mechanism is designed to prioritize instances with high confidence in their correct classification and low confidence in their correct classification, thereby enabling the model to learn from its weaknesses. Furthermore, a dual-stream network architecture is proposed to enhance the model's ability to generalize, with each stream focusing on distinct aspects of the data: one stream is optimized for recognizing common driving patterns and the other for detecting rare and complex scenarios. This method is evaluated on the NDS dataset and compared with leading self-training and pseudo-labeling techniques, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation metrics.

Evolutionary algorithms face a significant challenge in parallel computing due to the time it takes for each individual to be evaluated, which can result in slower convergence when using parallel approaches.  In this study, we investigate the impact of the difference in evaluation times on the performance of parallel evolutionary algorithms, specifically in terms of their efficiency and effectiveness.  We examine the Parallel Genetic Algorithm and the Parallel Differential Evolution methods, which are commonly used in multi-objective optimization tasks.  We also introduce a new parallel approach, Asynchronous Parallel Differential Evolution, which allows non-parallel methods to continue running in the background while parallel processing is performed in the foreground.  We test these algorithms under different evaluation time scenarios, which can be categorized into three distinct cases.  We find that the Asynchronous Parallel Differential Evolution method outperforms the other parallel algorithms in terms of solution quality, despite being slower due to the overhead of asynchronous operations.  We conclude that the choice of algorithm depends on the specific problem and the trade-off between solution quality and processing speed.

The discovery of TOI-1809b, a Neptune-sized exoplanet orbiting a star of approximately 0.9 solar masses, presents an intriguing case. This star-planet mass ratio sits at the crossroads where the planet-host mass-ratio power law shifts gears. As a result, TOI-1809b's mass ratio deviates significantly from the average, raising questions about its origins. Furthermore, its mass ratio is also at the threshold where the planet population splits into two distinct groups with varying metallicity characteristics. This phenomenon has implications for our understanding of the metallicity-mass relation in planetary systems.

This model is relevant to the study of superconducting circuits, where it can be used to model the dynamics of a qubit in a dissipative environment. The study of magnetism in heavy-fermion systems, particularly in the region where they coexist with ferromagnetism, is a significant area of research.  We have conducted an investigation into the magnetic properties of CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ using neutron diffraction and inelastic scattering, focusing on compositions between $x = 0.5$ and 0.8.  Our results indicate that the system exhibits ferromagnetic properties for $x \gtrapprox 0.6$.  Furthermore, the Curie temperatures range from 5.7 to 3.7 K, and the saturation magnetic moment increases with decreasing $x$ and shows a significant enhancement at $x = 0.5$.  Inelastic neutron scattering revealed a significant increase in the intensity of the magnetic Bragg peaks as the temperature decreased below the Curie temperature, and a comparison with the predicted intensity based on the domain wall width and the system's anisotropy constant revealed that the system is highly anisotropic.  These findings suggest that the system's magnetic properties are well-explained by a simple mean-field theory, and the system's anisotropy is likely to be the dominant factor influencing its behavior.

We conducted a search for HI narrow-line self-absorption (HINSA) in 15 high-mass star-forming regions using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope. The search covered the frequency range of 1.28 to 1.46 GHz and had a sensitivity of 0.75 mJy for a 20 km/s line width. The search did not yield any new HINSA detections, but we were able to confirm the HI narrow-line self-absorption in G035.58-022.61 and revise the luminosity of this source to 1.1 x 10^4 L_(\odot). The search also provided new upper limits on the luminosity of the sources studied. The upper limits were compared to the luminosity of the source G035.58-022.61 and were found to be consistent with the observed luminosity of the source. We demonstrate that certain properties of intermediate beta-transformations can be inferred from the properties of a related transformation involving a hole at zero in a greedy beta-model.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from mixing-induced phenomena in Bs decays is a crucial aspect of understanding the parameters of the Standard Model's second-generation quark sector. The phase phi_s can be measured through the analysis of charge-conjugate-pair events in Bs-0 to J/Psi f0(1585) and Bs-0 to J/Psi f0(1370) processes, where a significant breakthrough occurred in 2013 with the observation of the CP-violating asymmetry in the S-wave amplitudes of these two processes by the LHCb experiment. The current study presents an updated measurement of phi_s based on 9 fb^-1 of data collected at a high-energy proton-proton collision experiment with a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The results show that phi_s is consistent with the Standard Model predictions and values obtained in other experiments.

Deep neural networks excel in extracting relevant features from input data, but they often struggle to adapt these learnings to datasets with different underlying characteristics. This cross-dataset generalization challenge is particularly significant in text-based applications, where datasets are frequently expanded with new domains by incorporating more labels. Our proposed method, Domain-Adaptive Language Model (DALM), aims to improve text classification models by retraining them on target datasets. This approach involves fine-tuning a pre-trained text encoder using a contrastive loss to align the encoder's representations for the expanded input data. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating DALM yields substantial performance gains in text-based cross-dataset adaptation, surpassing traditional fine-tuning methods.

A non-collinear set of points in the plane can be referred to as an arc if it contains no lines. In the context of finite fields, specifically $\mathbb{F}_q^2$, we investigate the maximum number of points that form an arc of a quadratic curve, where we also consider special cases such as power curves and specific types of quadratics like $y^2 + y + x^3 = 0$.
A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by counting the number of valid subsets of its vertices.

Graph Neural Networks have achieved remarkable success in various graph-related tasks, but the lack of effective explanation methods hinders their practical adoption. Existing explanation techniques primarily focus on generating post-hoc explanations, which are insufficient in providing comprehensive insights. In contrast, we introduce a novel approach that generates intrinsic explanations for GNN models by modifying the network architecture to disentangle key predictive features. Our method, called GNN-XPLAIN, yields explanations that are more relevant, relevant to the underlying data, and can be optimized using a hybrid approach combining optimization and approximation techniques. Experimental results on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method over state-of-the-art approaches in terms of explanation quality and quantity.

We present X-ray and radio data for the cluster of galaxies RXCJ0232.2-4420, obtained at the MAST/VTT and Chandra observatories. The cluster's X-ray data show a temperature of 5.5 keV and a relatively symmetric morphology with no significant substructures. A radio halo was detected at the center of the cluster, with its spectrum matching that of synchrotron radiation. The absence of a cooling core and the presence of a radio halo in RXCJ0232.2-4420 make it a unique system among galaxy clusters.

We introduce the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel component for building recurrent neural networks (RNNs) that outperforms state-of-the-art models, including LSTMs and the transformer, in terms of both efficiency and effectiveness. The LMU's unique properties enable it to capture long-term patterns in data, while avoiding the computational and storage issues associated with traditional RNNs. By integrating the LMU into a simple RNN architecture, we achieve significant gains in accuracy, as evidenced by our results on a range of benchmark datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and IMDB.

The search for feebly interacting particles, including dark matter, is a key area of study in the field of fundamental physics.  The FIPSE initiative, a collaboration between the LHC and particle physics communities, has established a research agenda focused on detecting these particles.  This document outlines the research goals and objectives of FIPSE, providing a detailed roadmap for future research.  The document is divided into three sections, covering the motivation for the research, the design of experiments, and the potential scientific outcomes.  The research goals outlined in this document are designed to be both specific and achievable, with a focus on advancing our understanding of feebly interacting particles.

Language is deeply intertwined with human culture, yet the underlying processes driving language change over time are still not fully understood. In this research, we investigate how language evolves through migration by creating a model where individuals with unique languages move and interact with each other. Our model reveals that migration can isolate monolingual communities and that the rate of language adoption is significantly influenced by the size of these communities. Interestingly, our findings indicate that smaller monolingual communities are more effective in promoting language shift compared to larger ones. Furthermore, our model shows that the probability of multiple languages coexisting in a population is higher than would be expected by applying the principle of detailed balance.

We've developed a novel approach to training neural networks for solving complex partial differential equations with limited data, leveraging the Fourier cature technique to optimize the training process. Our method, known as the Fourier-Optimized Neural Networks (FONN), enables the creation of neural networks that are specifically designed to handle equations with specific high-frequency characteristics. By doing so, FONN can achieve faster convergence and improved accuracy on a range of test cases, even when the available data is limited. Interestingly, our results show that increasing the network's width actually hampers performance when dealing with high-frequency features, whereas a more sophisticated activation function is beneficial in this context.

This research investigates the decay of solutions in a two-wave system, comprising one wave equation with Kelvin-Voigt damping and another without. The combination of these systems results in a damped system, where one wave is partially damped and the other is not. By leveraging the exponential stability of the partially damped wave and the uniform stability of the completely undamped wave, we demonstrate the uniform exponential stability of the coupled system under certain conditions.

Deep reinforcement learning has achieved significant success in various complex tasks, but its applications in real-world scenarios are hindered by two major limitations: 1) it often relies on extensive trial-and-error experiments, which is impractical and infeasible in many cases; 2) it frequently requires large-scale computational resources, which is not only costly but also unsustainable. To address these issues, we introduce a new approach that leverages pre-trained deep neural networks to accelerate and improve the training process of reinforcement learning agents. Specifically, we propose a method that transfers knowledge from pre-trained networks to target tasks, which not only reduces the need for costly experiments but also makes the training process more sustainable by utilizing renewable resources such as GPU and CPU. Our approach also offers a level of robustness against noisy data, making it a valuable tool in real-world scenarios where data is often imperfect.

A technique to produce optical nonreciprocity in a ring resonator system using quantum squeezing is proposed. This method leverages squeezing and inverse squeezing of two coupled resonator modes to create unidirectional transmission. Quantum squeezing can be realized by engineering non-Hermitian systems with balanced loss and gain, or by utilizing parametric amplification. We demonstrate that in a system with two coupled resonators, optical nonreciprocity can be achieved with minimal requirements, involving only two pump lasers. This system enables unidirectional transmission with identical input powers at both ports, and allows for flexible adjustment of transmission ratios.

The CRESST experiment employs a unique approach to study dark matter interactions by utilizing scintillation and zeolite-based radiopurity measurements within a cryogenic detector. This approach allows for the identification of dark matter signals even in the presence of radioactive interference, given that the scintillation signal has a distinct appearance compared to dark matter signals. Furthermore, the scintillation readout enhances the experiment's sensitivity to dark matter particles weighing less than 1 GeV/c$^2$.

We introduce a novel kernel mixture model for restoring blurred images in an inpainting context, where the blur kernel is composed of multiple Gaussian kernels with varying scales. To address the challenges of estimating the number of kernels and their parameters, we propose a non-parametric Bayesian approach based on the Dirichlet process prior. To facilitate efficient computation, we employ a stochastic Expectation-Maximization algorithm, which alternates between sampling the kernel mixture configuration and optimizing the signal and kernel parameters. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in estimating the blur kernel configuration and achieving superior restoration performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a new concept of associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight (λ,γ) and shows its connection to the double curved Rota-Baxter system, establishing a BiHom-Loday-Leibniz algebra structure and its associated BiHom-pre-Loday-Leibniz algebra with weight λ. Additionally, we define and study the cohomology of the associated BiHom-Loday-Leibniz algebra and its pre-algebra counterpart.

Formal verification via Hoare logic is widely employed in software creation, yet its application in concurrent systems remains limited. A major reason for this limitation is the absence of a straightforward, automated method for verifying concurrent programs using Hoare logic. This paper presents a novel approach to automatic verification of concurrent programs utilizing Hoare logic and parallelism. This method views the verification problem as a decidable game involving a graph, allowing for the use of graph-theoretic techniques to ensure soundness. Our approach also enables the application of graph-theoretic techniques to solve the verification problem, making it computationally efficient. This paper showcases the effectiveness of our approach by verifying a real-world example, a concurrent implementation of the classic producer-consumer problem.

Distributed consensus is a critical component for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly.  Existing research has primarily focused on either high-performance or high-assurance distributed consensus protocols, but there is a lack of work that balances both goals.  This paper proposes Canopus, a distributed consensus protocol that achieves high performance and high assurance by utilizing a novel combination of atomic block transfers and novel fault detection methods.  Canopus is designed to work with existing fault detection mechanisms, and we demonstrate its effectiveness in a real-world setting, showing that it can be used to replicate a distributed database while providing high-assurance fault detection.

The molecular structure of a lipid bilayer's undulatory pattern is examined using a free-energy based approach that incorporates the van der Waals attraction between adjacent lipids. It's found that this pattern minimizes the energy associated with the van der Waals attraction by maximizing the area between lipid molecules, resulting in a well-defined undulatory length scale. The effects of lipid molecule geometry and molecular interactions on this length scale are then investigated. It's also demonstrated that introducing cholesterol into a lipid bilayer reduces its bending rigidity by altering its interstitial lipid content, resulting in a length scale shift.

This paper delves into the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian, which is derived from the loop quantum gravity framework. We examine the LQC model created using the reduced minisuperspace model, which incorporates scale factor uncertainty and a cosmological constant. We derive the LQC model's critical matter density, which marks the threshold for quantum gravity effects to emerge, and find that it aligns with the loop quantum cosmological model based on the Wilson loop approach. Furthermore, we investigate the quantum cosmological evolution of the LQC model, which exhibits a Big Bounce behavior, and identify the conditions under which the LQC model can produce inflation following the bounce.

The Pierre Auger Observatory has documented the energy spectra of the most energetic cosmic rays observed on Earth, spanning an energy range from $10^{17.6}$ to $10^{20.1}$ eV.  This paper details the primary findings from the southern hemisphere component of the observatory, covering an area of 2.9 square kilometers, and presents the results of the accompanying statistical analysis.

Deep neural networks have made significant advancements in solving complex computer vision tasks, but their practical use in robotics is hindered by issues with output noise and inconsistencies. This problem can be viewed as a regression challenge, where we need to develop a way to reduce output noise and ensure consistency. In this research, we present a new method of training deep neural networks, called Deep Regression Consistency Training (DRCT), which can help eliminate output noise and ensure consistency. The method works by utilizing a small, randomly selected data perturbation to retrain the network's final layer, using the original output as a reference point. The results of our experiments, which involved testing our approach on multiple datasets and against various baselines, demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing output noise and increasing prediction consistency.

Predicting traffic flow from time-series traffic data is a crucial application of machine learning in intelligent transportation systems. However, traffic data is inherently complex and noisy, making it prone to overfitting when using deep learning models. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages spatially cropped patches of test data to assess model robustness. By testing a model's performance on different days with the same patches, we can gauge its ability to handle changes in traffic patterns. Through this patch-based evaluation, we can identify potential weaknesses in the model and refine its performance. Experimental results on real-world traffic datasets demonstrate that this patch-based approach significantly improves the model's robustness and generalization capabilities.

Gray categories were originally conceived as a compromise between 2-categories and double categories. However, it's been realized that Gray categories can also be seen as a specific type of 3-category where faces and mates satisfy certain conditions. This realization allows us to build on the theory of 3-categories to develop a comprehensive theory of Gray categories, which in turn enables the extension of 2-categories and double categories in a consistent manner.

Accurate hippocampus segmentation from brain imaging data is crucial for understanding neuropsychiatric disorders and could be enhanced by machine learning techniques. However, current fully automated methods often require large amounts of labeled data and may not perform well in diverse populations. A proposed solution involves training a model on a smaller dataset and then fine-tuning it with the help of a human expert, leveraging their knowledge to compensate for any data-related limitations. In this context, an advanced model based on 3D U-Net architecture has been developed to segment hippocampus images, and its potential for adapting to new datasets has been explored. The model achieved high segmentation accuracy when applied to a new dataset, and combining it with human input resulted in even better performance. These findings suggest that integrating human and machine expertise can be a successful strategy for improving medical image analysis.

We've successfully implemented the quantum zeno paradox in an optical setup where three parties navigate a two-path interferometer without any two sharing a path, utilizing the entanglement of two photons. Our setup allows for the measurement of the entangled photons' state without disturbing it, enabling the effective "freezing" of the interferometer's evolution and preserving its initial output. Our findings align with a theoretical model and offer a new approach to studying the quantum zeno effect in optical systems.

The inner proton radiation belt, extending from low-Earth orbit to geostationary orbit, has long been a subject of debate. Research has primarily focused on the outer radiation belt, with the inner radiation belt's origin remaining unclear. A recent study suggests that a transient mechanism is responsible for the inner radiation belt's formation. The researchers propose that a transient mechanism can explain the inner radiation belt's characteristics, including its unique spatial distribution and temporal stability. The mechanism's effectiveness is supported by observations of proton radiation and tracers such as carbon and oxygen. The study's findings indicate that a transient mechanism can create radiation belts with energy levels up to 50 keV, aligning with the inner radiation belt's energy range. The mechanism's persistence is attributed to the continuous injection of particles from the inner magnetosphere, with the particles' energy levels influenced by the inner radiation belt's spatial distribution. The study's results provide new insights into the inner radiation belt's formation and the mechanisms driving radiation belt dynamics.

Deep neural networks' performance limitations can be attributed to their expressivity, which is influenced by their architecture. By analyzing the expressivity of deep neural networks through a linear algebraic lens, researchers can pinpoint the inherent constraints that dictate their capabilities. This expressivity perspective enables the development of more effective architectures, which can be achieved by designing networks that are optimally expressive given a fixed parameter budget. A key challenge in optimizing expressivity is that the underlying expressivity constraints are complex and difficult to analyze. However, by casting expressivity constraints as semidefinite programs, which are computationally intensive problems, researchers can derive insights into the nature of these constraints. This insight can be leveraged to simplify the optimization of expressivity and develop more effective architectures.

This paper presents an innovative approach to secure low-rank matrix completion, 
where a user uploads a noisy version of a matrix's entries to an untrusted server, 
which attempts to recover the original matrix. The server processes the data 
using an optimization method that incorporates a loss function and regularization terms, 
but the user has no control over the choice of parameters. To address this issue, 
we propose a new algorithm that ensures privacy by using the Huber loss function 
and a specific form of regularization that can be chosen securely by the user. 
The user encrypts a noise vector and sends it to the server, which, due to the 
robustness properties of the Huber loss, is unable to determine the noise vector's 
direction. The server's inability to recover the original matrix is proven under 
certain conditions, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through 
experiments that compare its performance with other existing methods.

The interstellar medium contains a mysterious component that is essential for understanding various celestial phenomena, specifically the dust that is present in every phase of star formation and plays a crucial role in the lifecycle of galaxies. Although the interstellar medium contains a mixture of different substances, scientists have made significant progress in understanding its composition by analyzing observations from space-based telescopes. One key component of the interstellar medium is polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, specifically large PAHs with 3-6 carbon atoms in their molecular structure. These large PAHs are thought to be a major component of interstellar dust, but their exact role remains unclear. In this study, scientists have used computer simulations to model the behavior of large PAHs in different interstellar environments and observed how they interact with each other. The simulations showed that large PAHs are capable of forming complex structures in space, specifically spiral and star-shaped formations, and that they can easily transfer energy and merge with other PAHs. The study also found that large PAHs are more resistant to destruction than smaller PAHs and can survive for long periods of time in various interstellar environments. The researchers concluded that large PAHs are a key component of interstellar dust and play a crucial role in understanding various celestial phenomena.

The discovery of planets around low-mass stars is a rapidly evolving field.  Theoretical models suggest that planets can form around stars as small as 0.1 solar masses, but this is still unconfirmed due to the lack of observational data.  The TESS mission has recently discovered two planets orbiting low-mass stars, but their masses are uncertain.  The aim of this study is to investigate the minimum mass of planets that can be detected by TESS around low-mass stars using data from the MUNI survey.  The MUNI survey observed 85 low-mass stars using TESS, and we used the TessOptimize transit detection algorithm to identify 11 planets.  The study found that all 11 planets have radii between 1.5 and 3.5 times that of the Earth, and orbital periods between 5 and 30 days.  The minimum mass of the planets was estimated using the OTOI method, and we found that all 11 planets have minimum masses greater than 2.5 times that of the Earth.  The study suggests that planets with radii less than 2.5 times that of the Earth can be detected around low-mass stars with periods less than 20 days.  The study also found that planets with minimum masses greater than 10 times that of the Earth can be detected around low-mass stars with periods less than 30 days. This research introduces a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model that integrates image restoration techniques, specifically designed to handle noisy images and "blind spots" – areas with missing pixel information. By addressing these issues through image restoration methods, the model can effectively segment different object categories within an image. A multi-stage approach is adopted, with each stage comprising a deep learning-based image restoration model and an image segmentation model. The image restoration stage utilizes a pre-trained model to restore noisy images and identify potential object boundaries, while the image segmentation stage leverages the restored image and boundary map to segment objects of interest. A novel training method is proposed to synchronize the multi-stage model, with a theoretical analysis provided to demonstrate its convergence. Experimental results demonstrate the model's ability to segment images with significant noise and missing pixel information, outperforming existing state-of-the-art image segmentation models in various benchmark datasets.
